title: How Costco Makes $9 Billion While Barely Profiting From Products
description:
Costco sold about $297 billion of products in fiscal 2026, yet the products themselves earned it only about 2 cents of operating profit per dollar. The real engine is membership: $5.9 billion in fees, less than 2% of revenue but about half of operating profit. Here's how the model works, how it started, what could break it, and what it means for you as a shopper.

Sources:
- Costco FY2026 Q4 and full-year results (52 weeks ended Aug 30, 2026): https://investor.costco.com
- Costco FY2026 Form 10-K (members, renewal rates, Executive share of sales, SKUs, warehouses): https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000909832
- Membership fee increase effective Sept 1, 2024 (Costco announcement)
Markup caps are as reported by press and analysts, not company filings.

For education only. Not financial or investment advice.

scenes.say: Last year, Costco sold almost three hundred billion dollars worth of stuff. And on all those products, it made almost nothing.
Yet the company still made over nine billion dollars in profit. So where does the money actually come from?
The answer is one of the smartest business models in the world. And once you see it, you'll start spotting it everywhere.

visual.title: How Costco Makes Money
visual.sub: the business model hiding in plain sight

scenes.say: Chapter one. The strange math.
Costco's total revenue last year was just over three hundred and three billion dollars. Almost all of it came from selling products.

Now follow the money. Start with the revenue. Take away what Costco paid for the products themselves. Then take away the cost of running the business: staff, warehouses, trucks. What's left is operating profit, about eleven point seven billion.
That's a profit of less than four cents on every dollar that comes in. Thin, for a company this famous.
And membership fees? Only five point nine billion dollars. Less than two percent of revenue.

visual.label: of revenue came from membership fees

scenes.say: But here's the twist. Those same fees made up about half of Costco's operating profit.

visual.title: Membership fees as a share of...

scenes.say: Split the profit pie and it looks like this. One half from fees. The other half from three hundred billion dollars of shopping.

Try a thought experiment. If Costco stopped charging fees tomorrow and changed nothing else, its operating profit would fall from about eleven point seven billion to under six billion. Half the company's profit, gone.
In other words, Costco isn't really in the business of selling you groceries. It's in the business of selling you a membership card.

visual.text:
Not a grocery store.
A membership business.

scenes.say: Chapter two. Prices on purpose.
Costco reportedly caps its markup at fourteen percent on most brands, and fifteen percent on its own Kirkland brand.
You can see it in the numbers. For every dollar of products Costco sold, it paid about eighty-nine cents to buy them. It kept only about eleven cents to run the entire company.
Costco's own annual report says it runs on significantly lower margins than most other retailers. That's not an accident. It's the strategy.

visual.text:
"Significantly lower gross margins
than most other retailers"

scenes.say: After paying for staff, buildings and shipping, the products themselves leave Costco about two cents of operating profit per dollar sold.
That's why the famous one dollar fifty hot dog and soda combo hasn't changed price since nineteen eighty-five. Cheap prices aren't a mistake. They're the marketing.

visual.sub: hot dog + soda · same price since 1985

scenes.say: Every time a news story says the hot dog is still a dollar fifty, Costco gets free advertising. It tells you, before you walk in, that prices here are fair.

visual.title: What a $1.50 hot dog buys Costco

scenes.say: Chapter three. The membership machine.
Costco now has about eighty-four million paid members. A basic Gold Star membership in the US costs sixty-five dollars a year. Executive costs one hundred and thirty.

visual.title: Who pays Costco to shop there

scenes.say: And that number keeps climbing. In just two years, Costco added almost eight million paid members.
Membership fees are almost pure profit. There's no product to buy, no shelf to stock. And members pay upfront, before they've bought a single thing.

visual.title: Why fees are the perfect revenue

scenes.say: They also renew. In the US and Canada, about ninety-two percent of members renew. Worldwide, about ninety percent.
Put another way: out of every hundred members in the US and Canada, about ninety-two come back the next year and pay again. Most subscription businesses would love a number like that.
Then there's the upgrade. About half of paid members now pay for Executive. And those Executive members account for about three quarters of all Costco sales.

visual.title: Executive members
visual.verdict: The biggest shoppers pay the biggest fee

scenes.say: Because people renew so reliably, Costco can even raise the fee. In September twenty twenty-four, Gold Star went from sixty to sixty-five dollars, and Executive from one twenty to one thirty. Most members simply paid it.
Partly as a result, membership fee income grew about eleven percent last year, to five point nine billion dollars.
That means Costco knows, a year in advance, where roughly half of its operating profit will come from. Investors pay a lot for that kind of predictability.

visual.title: Profit Costco can count on before the year starts

scenes.say: Chapter four. The flywheel.

Low prices attract more members. More members means Costco buys in enormous volume. Huge volume lets it negotiate lower costs from suppliers. And lower costs mean even lower prices. Then the loop starts again.
Costco also keeps its range tiny. Fewer than four thousand items per warehouse, while a typical supermarket carries tens of thousands.
Fewer items means much bigger orders of each one. That gives Costco enormous bargaining power, and it makes the warehouses simpler and cheaper to run.
And the stores themselves are bare warehouses. Concrete floors, products on pallets, no fancy displays. Every saving goes back into lower prices, which feeds the flywheel again.
Kirkland Signature, Costco's own brand, adds another turn. Costco controls the product, so it can sell high quality at a lower price, and build loyalty no other store can copy.

visual.label: Costco's own brand
visual.sub: a growing share of sales, per the 10-K

scenes.say: Chapter five. How it started.
The idea is older than Costco. In nineteen seventy-six, Sol Price opened Price Club in San Diego, one of the first membership warehouses.
His insight was simple. Charge a small fee to join, keep prices barely above cost, and the people who pay to get in will come back again and again to get their money's worth.
Costco opened its first warehouse in Seattle in nineteen eighty-three, copying the model and pushing it further. Ten years later, the two companies merged.
Today, Costco runs nine hundred and thirty-nine warehouses. Most are in the United States, but there are more than a hundred in Canada and more than a hundred and seventy in other countries.
Chapter six. What could go wrong?
No model is bulletproof. The biggest risk is simple. If members stop renewing, half the profit is at stake.
There's also competition. Rival warehouse clubs, and online stores that deliver bulk goods to your door, all fight for the same shoppers.

visual.title: Pressure points
items: Fee hikes that go too far

scenes.say: Growth is the other question. Costco grows mainly by opening new warehouses and signing up new members. That works for decades, but every new building costs money, and the best locations get taken first.

visual.title: Paid members (millions)
visual.note: Growth so far is steady, but it must be earned year after year

scenes.say: And Costco can only push the fee so far. Raise it too much, and the deal stops feeling like a deal. That's why increases have been small and years apart.

visual.text:
The fee only works
while the deal feels fair.

scenes.say: Chapter seven. What it means for you.

First, as a shopper. Is a basic membership even worth it? It depends on how much you save. Say Costco saves you five percent compared with your usual store. That's just an example; your savings could be higher or lower.

visual.label: example saving vs your usual store
visual.sub: an assumption, not a Costco figure

scenes.say: At five percent, you'd need to spend about thirteen hundred dollars a year, roughly a hundred and ten a month, just to win back the sixty-five dollar fee.
And watch out for the bulk trap. A cheaper price per unit only saves you money if you actually use it all. Thirty-six rolls you need is a deal. A giant tub of food you throw away is not.

visual.title: The bulk-buying trap
visual.verdict: Price per unit used is what counts

scenes.say: Now the upgrade. Executive gives two percent back on most purchases. The upgrade costs sixty-five dollars more, so it only pays off if you spend over three thousand two hundred and fifty dollars a year at Costco.
Here's how that plays out. Spend two thousand a year, and you get forty dollars back. Not worth it. Spend six thousand, and you get one hundred and twenty. That's fifty-five dollars ahead.
The reward is capped at one thousand two hundred and fifty dollars a year, which you'd only hit by spending sixty-two thousand five hundred. Most households are nowhere near that.

visual.label: spend needed to hit the $1,250 reward cap

scenes.say: Second, as someone learning how business works. The best businesses often don't profit from what they sell. They profit from the relationship. Think Amazon Prime, gyms, or software subscriptions.
So next time you see a business with surprisingly low prices, ask: what are they really selling? Often, it's access.

visual.text:
Low prices?
Ask what they're really selling.

scenes.say: Costco sells products at almost no profit, and charges you for the right to shop. That's the whole secret.
